activities.description: Clarke discusses his experience as the Parliamentary Poet Laureate and the controversy surrounding his initial lack of assignments. He argues that poetry is a powerful art form that should be utilized more effectively in political contexts. He describes the news coverage of his complaints and his subsequent influx of requests to write poems. He recounts reciting poems in Parliament and for government officials. He concludes by emphasizing the inherent power and resilience of poetry.

characterInteraction.description: Thomson poses a question to Clarke, prompting him to share his experience. The dynamic is primarily focused on Clarke's narration with occasional affirmations from Thomson.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Clarke's experience highlights the potential for poetry to be a powerful tool for social commentary and political engagement. His frustration with initial constraints underscores the importance of artists being able to freely express their voices.

keyMoments.changeDescription: Clarke's tone becomes more animated as he directly addresses the parliamentarians. The shift from reflective narration to direct address creates a more energetic feel.
Clarke's laughter and exclamations ('Come on! Come on!') contribute to a sense of excitement as he emphasizes poetry's political relevance.

narrativeProgression.description: Clarke details his initial frustrations as Poet Laureate, the subsequent media attention, and his newfound sense of purpose in leveraging poetry for political engagement.
Clarke reveals his frustration with the lack of requests to write poetry.
He explains that he felt constrained and unable to fully express his voice.
He recounts the news coverage of his complaints and how it reached a national audience.
He describes receiving his first request to write a poem after the news broke.
He expresses excitement about the opportunity to recite poems in Parliament.

scenes.thematicElements: The power of poetry, political engagement, marginalization of art, freedom of expression.
scenes.title: George Elliott Clarke's Experience as Parliamentary Poet Laureate

was marked with one's little controversy, but near the end of my first year, it was October 2016,
when I finally just got fed up with the way things were going. Because I had been poet laureate of
Toronto 2012-2015 and I had been able to recite a poem every April National Poetry Month for the City
Council. I thought that was very important and I had tried to inject myself as a poet into various
public enterprises of one sort or another under the City of Toronto. And I got some pushback.
I also got some acceptance here and there. And so I felt that I was the seventh
parliamentary poet laureate. I thought, okay, it's time to make sure that we poets can actually have
a real public role in this position. And I felt that I felt constrained. I felt that I wasn't
being permitted to say what I really wanted to say or address things I really wanted to address
because some functionaries believe that I could cause a controversy if I said something that would
get the Library of Parliament or the government itself into trouble in some way, shape, or form.
So it was better that I be as muscled as possible. And so I put up with that until October when I
mentioned to a CBC reporter in Halifax, I was not having a great time as poet laureate because I
wasn't being asked to write anything. Members of parliament, senators, ministers, nobody was
asking me to write a poem. And I figured that as the parliament you poet laureate, I'm an officer
of parliament. I'm responsible to parliament. So, yo, parliamentarians, you might want to make
use of my talent here. I can always say no if I don't like what you're asking me to do or write,
I can say no. But I'm here as your poet laureate. So you should be thinking about things I might want
to address as your poet laureate. So the news broke on October 5th, 2016. It was national news.
I happened to be in Good old Scotland on that date. In fact, I was giving a reading at the Scottish
poetry library in Edinburgh, along with some other poets, British and American. And I was the sole
Canadian involved in that particular moment. So I was out of the country when the news broke and
it was a little tempest in a tea pot that the poet laureate is upset at the parliamentarians

I got my first request from a number of parliament to write a poem that was read in parliament.
I didn't get to read any poems in parliament. I had several poems read in the House of Commons
and in the Senate, which for me was that's the gold standard. That's the gold standard. Somebody

I got a member of parliament. You don't need to. I got the Queen's printer publishing it for
crying out loud. I got a minister of the crown reciting a poem. Come on. That's power. That's
power. I don't know. Gee, what is? Yes, poetry is marginalized in the ways that power moves
in the ways that money moves and accumulates and gets disposed of here and there and so on. But
poetry is that secret resistant art that never goes away. It's always the gorilla art. It's always

youtube_description:
George Elliott Clarke recounts the minor controversy he caused as Poet Laureate of Canada, and having his poetry read in the House of Commons.

Interviewed by R.H. Thomson on May 10, 2019 in Toronto. 
Filming location courtesy of Cahoots Theatre
Produced with the support of the City of Toronto through the Toronto Arts Council
